passage: At the colony park after school, Parul held out her hand toward Harish's packet of biscuits. "I will not share with you," Harish said, hugging it. "You are not my friend." Parul's chest went tight and her eyes stung. "That makes me sad," she said quietly. She did not grab. She walked to the swings and pushed one by herself. Later the teacher, who had been watching from the gate, called them over to talk about taking turns.

qa.q: What did Harish say to Parul about the biscuits?
qa.a: He said, "I will not share with you. You are not my friend."

qa.q: How was Parul feeling when her chest went tight and her eyes stung?
qa.a: She felt hurt and sad about being rejected. She named it when she said, "That makes me sad."

qa.q: What did Parul do that kept the moment from turning into a fight?
qa.a: She said how she felt, did not grab, and went to play elsewhere. Later the teacher helped the two of them think about taking turns.

qa.q: How might Harish see the moment when Parul reached for his biscuits?
qa.a: He probably feels protective of his own snack and afraid of losing it, and used a harsh line he does not fully mean. He may not realise how much it stung.

grounding: A friend says he will not share and that she is not his friend; it stings, and she says she is sad and plays elsewhere.

passage: Note from Sudha, class teacher. Today I said "Mohit!" sharply in front of everyone when he tore a page in the story book. His face went red, his chin dropped and he pulled his collar up to his ears. He did not speak for the rest of circle time. I realised my tone had made him want to hide. Afterwards I knelt at his desk and said quietly, "Books are for gentle hands. Shall we mend the page together?" He nodded and reached for the tape.

qa.q: What did Mohit tear in the story book?
qa.a: He tore a page.

qa.q: What did Mohit's red face and raised collar suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest shame and a wish to hide. His silence for the rest of circle time points the same way.

qa.q: What did Sudha change after seeing how Mohit reacted?
qa.a: She spoke to him quietly after class and offered a chance to fix the page together, instead of scolding in public.

qa.q: How might Mohit's classmates have seen the sharp call of his name?
qa.a: They probably felt tense and may have been afraid of being called out too. It can teach them to hide mistakes rather than to fix them.

grounding: The teacher says my name sternly in front of the class and my face burns; a quiet talk afterwards with a chance to fix it is wiser.

passage: Rashmi gripped her pencil in her fist and pressed so hard that the tip snapped. Her ears went warm. Ma'am came and crouched. "Let me show you again." She moved Rashmi's fingers to pinch near the tip and smiled. "Try now." The line wobbled, then straightened. Rashmi drew a letter A, slowly, and turned to Yash beside her. "Look, my A!" She did not feel judged at all, only helped.

qa.q: What happened to Rashmi's pencil when she pressed hard?
qa.a: The tip snapped.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel about the teacher's correction?
qa.a: She felt helped, not judged, and took pride in her letter. Her excitement in showing Yash the A shows it.

qa.q: What does Rashmi learn about mistakes from this moment?
qa.a: Being corrected is part of learning and does not mean she is bad, so she tries again. 😊

qa.q: How might Yash see Rashmi after the teacher's help?
qa.a: He sees her light up about her A. Seeing a calm correction may make him less afraid to ask for help himself.

grounding: The teacher gently shows me how to hold the pencil and smiles; I feel helped, not judged, and try again with pride.

passage: Note from the class teacher. Today I saw Uday throw a paper plane and told him off. He went silent and scowled at his shoes, arms crossed, and would not join the drawing. When I sat by him later he said, "Harsha threw one too and you only said me." I had not seen Harsha's. I thanked Uday for telling me and said I was sorry I had not looked at both. Then I spoke to the two of them together. Uday's frown eased a little.

qa.q: What did Uday throw before the teacher told him off?
qa.a: He threw a paper plane.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when he scowled and sat with crossed arms?
qa.a: He felt that being told off alone was unfair, and he was cross and hurt. His silence shows how much.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped, and what could Uday try next time?
qa.a: They sat by him, listened to his side, thanked him and apologised for not looking at both. Uday could speak up sooner, without sulking, if he thinks it is unfair.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt when the teacher spoke to both boys together?
qa.a: Harsha may have been uneasy, relieved or a bit guilty at being included. It was fairer because both had done the same thing.

grounding: I was scolded for something my friend also did; it feels unfair and I go quiet, and a wise adult listens to my side.

passage: Leela was racing along the wet corridor when Seema Ma'am's voice stopped her. "Leela, walking feet. The floor is wet and you could slip." Leela slowed, her cheeks warm. She looked up at the calm face. Ma'am is not cross because she dislikes me, she thought. She wants me safe. "Sorry, Ma'am. I will do better." Ma'am smiled and squeezed her shoulder, and Leela walked the rest of the way carefully.

qa.q: What did Seema Ma'am tell Leela about the floor?
qa.a: She said, "The floor is wet and you could slip."

qa.q: What did Leela think about why Ma'am corrected her?
qa.a: She thought Ma'am was not cross because she dislikes her, but wants her safe. That trust let her say sorry easily.

qa.q: What makes Leela able to hear the correction and still feel loved?
qa.a: The teacher gave a short reason, spoke calmly and smiled and squeezed her shoulder afterwards. Leela knew the concern was about safety.

qa.q: How might Seema Ma'am feel when Leela says "I will do better"?
qa.a: She is probably glad that Leela took the correction well and that the safety point was understood. The squeeze on the shoulder shows warmth.

grounding: I know my teacher corrects me because she cares whether I am safe; I can say sorry and still feel loved.

passage:
"Amma, Ma'am laughed at my letter." Aditi's voice was small.
"Which letter, beta?" said Ishita.
"I wrote it backwards. She called me silly and everybody laughed. I don't want to go to school."
Ishita pulled her close. "That must have felt awful. It is not your fault. Everyone writes letters backwards while learning."
"Will Ma'am be cross?"
"I will go and talk to her. You told me, and that was right."

qa.q: What did Aditi write backwards?
qa.a: She wrote a letter backwards.

qa.q: What is Aditi feeling when she says she does not want to go to school?
qa.a: She feels small and afraid of school, because she was laughed at and called silly in front of everyone.

qa.q: What did Ishita do that helps Aditi after the humiliation?
qa.a: She listened, said it was not Aditi's fault, and promised to talk to the teacher. Telling a parent was the right step. 🤍

qa.q: How might Ishita be feeling as she listens to her daughter?
qa.a: She is probably worried and protective, and wants to keep Aditi from feeling ashamed. Her calm voice hides that from Aditi.

grounding: A teacher laughs at my mistake and calls me silly in front of everyone; I feel small and afraid, and telling a parent helps.

passage: I am Simran and I sit next to Maria. Today our teacher said, "Well done, Maria, you tried so hard on that sum," and stuck a gold star on her page. Maria sat up straight and her cheeks went pink. She looked at the star for a long time. At break she asked for the harder page instead of the easy one. I do not know what she felt exactly, but she looked tall and happy to me.

qa.q: What did the teacher stick on Maria's page?
qa.a: The teacher stuck a gold star on her page.

qa.q: What does Maria's choice of the harder page suggest about how the praise affected her?
qa.a: It suggests she felt proud and keen to keep trying, because she was praised for effort. She did not seem afraid of a mistake.

qa.q: Why is "you tried so hard" a better kind of praise than "you are the best"?
qa.a: It tells her that effort is what counts, so a mistake does not threaten her. Praise only for being best can make a child fear errors. 😊

qa.q: How does Simran's own account limit what we can know about Maria?
qa.a: Simran only saw Maria's straight back, pink cheeks and choice, and says she does not know exactly what she felt. It is an outside guess.

grounding: The teacher says well done, you tried so hard, and gives me a star; I feel tall and happy and want to keep trying.

passage:
"Papa, look!" Vinita held up her foot. The laces were tied in a lumpy bow.
"Vinita! You did it yourself!"
"I made the loops. Then I pulled."
"I can see how carefully you did it." Tejas hugged her. "I am proud of you."
"Can I do the other one?"
"Yes, please." Tejas smiled. "And when your shoes are untied I love you exactly the same."
"I know, Papa."

qa.q: How did Vinita tie her laces?
qa.a: She made the loops and then pulled.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling when she asked, "Can I do the other one?"
qa.a: She was proud, excited and eager to do more, because her father's hug and praise made her feel safe and loved.

qa.q: What did Tejas add at the end that goes beyond praising the shoes?
qa.a: He told her he loves her exactly the same when her shoes are untied, so she learns she is loved for who she is, not only for what she does. 😊

qa.q: How might Tejas feel watching Vinita show her laces?
qa.a: He is probably delighted and proud, and moved that his daughter wanted to show him first.

grounding: My parent hugs me and says 'I am proud of you' after I tie my shoes; I feel safe, loved and eager to show more.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof, so break was indoors and the classroom was loud and cramped. The teacher held up Nitin's drawing of a boat. "Lovely work, Nitin." Hafsa frowned across the desks. "You are not that good." Nitin's smile slipped. His stomach felt twisty and his eyes stung, and the rain and shouting made it harder to think. He did not brag or snap back. He said, "I like your drawing too, Hafsa," and picked up his crayons.

qa.q: Why was break indoors?
qa.a: The rain drummed on the tin roof, so break was indoors.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when his smile slipped after Hafsa's remark?
qa.a: He felt puzzled and hurt, with a twisty stomach, since he had just been praised and then criticised.

qa.q: What did Nitin do that stayed kind without bragging?
qa.a: He did not brag or snap back, but told Hafsa he liked her drawing too. That left the moment calm.

qa.q: What might Hafsa be feeling when she frowned and said "You are not that good"?
qa.a: She may be feeling envy, wishing that she had been praised. It is her feeling, not proof that Nitin did wrong.

grounding: After the teacher praises me, a classmate frowns and says I am not that good; I stay kind and do not brag.

passage: Note from Pallavi's class teacher, after the school function. Pallavi recited her poem about the monsoon and Dadi clapped loudest, then told the parents around her, "My Pallavi said a poem!" Pallavi's cheeks glowed but she hid half behind Dadi's sari and smiled shyly. When someone asked her to say it again, she looked at Dadi first. I quietly mentioned that Pallavi may like to choose when to recite. Dadi laughed and agreed. 🙂

qa.q: What did Pallavi recite at the function?
qa.a: She recited her poem about the monsoon.

qa.q: How was Pallavi feeling when she hid half behind Dadi's sari?
qa.a: She glowed with pride but also felt shy. Her smile and her hiding both show it.

qa.q: What did the teacher suggest, and why might it matter?
qa.a: The teacher said Pallavi may like to choose when to recite. That keeps the poem something she does for joy and not a show she must perform for approval.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel when she hears the teacher's suggestion?
qa.a: Dadi is probably proud and a little surprised. She laughed and agreed, so she took it warmly and wants Pallavi to enjoy the poem.

grounding: Dadi claps when I recite a poem and tells everyone; I glow and feel shy, and the pressure to perform is kept gentle.
